access.title: The Coal Woman's Measure
access.firstPersonText: Rosa Brandl arrived with coal in a cart that shed black water over my threshold. I asked her to place three baskets beneath the east stairs and she declined until she had inspected the floor. It was rotten, she said, and she would not have the collapse of an aristocratic ruin attributed to her horse. I informed her that the place possessed no aristocracy except the intellectual kind. She placed the coal in the kitchen instead, where its dust settled upon my clean papers. Her measure was tin, deeply dented, and indisputably honest. I paid more than I had intended, then watched her carry the final basket without the assistance I had neglected to offer. For three winters afterward she knew my fuel expenditure more accurately than any surviving colleague knew my work. She never called me Professor. Curiously, I did not correct her.

access.title: A Letter from Henry
access.firstPersonText: Henry wrote from somewhere beyond my immediate reach. His letter asked after the smaller creatures and whether I had found a way to maintain viable tissue at greater scale. It contained no offer to visit. I began a reply of forty pages and reduced it to four. I sent him observations on the limits of growth but refused the procedure he sought, although I could scarcely have given him one. At the end I added a line asking whether he had recovered from the quarrels of our final university months. I struck it out and wrote instead that the Queen continued to exhibit surprising preferences. He did not answer for several years. I kept his letter under the blue ledger where it left a pale rectangular mark.

access.title: The Terms of an Open Door
access.firstPersonText: Julian visited on his way through Bavaria, carrying no instrument at all. I regarded this as a disarming omission. We walked in the garden, where the nettles had appropriated a path I had intended to repair for years. He spoke of the life he had made in Vienna, of friends whose names were not familiar to me, and of a younger restorer to whom he had entrusted part of his business. I discovered that I had been treating his absence as a temporary condition which my next letter might end. He said he cared for me, but would not arrange his remaining years around a door which opened only when my experiments permitted. I objected to the theatricality of his metaphor and knew immediately that it was mine he had learned. He did not threaten to sever the connection. He asked only that I cease describing another person's independence as a betrayal. After his departure I had the neglected path cut back. I wrote to him describing the work, not pretending it had been done for an optical demonstration. He sent a short note asking whether the nettles would return. They have, repeatedly.

access.title: The Visit to Clara's Garden
access.firstPersonText: Clara had taken to keeping herbs and bees behind her house. I visited one July afternoon without needing a bottle, an instrument, or a favor. She asked my opinion of a sickly plant. I pronounced on its leaves, twice and incorrectly, until she lifted a paving stone and showed me how the roots had been crowded. We moved the stone, drank warm tea, and watched bees make an industry of the thyme. I spoke of the lives I had brought forth. Clara replied that her garden had never once obeyed her merely because she planted it. I said my case was rather different. She handed me the watering can without further dispute. The plant recovered. On my next visit I brought a drawing of its roots, and she used the reverse of the paper to write a shopping list.

access.title: The Visit to Clara's Garden
access.firstPersonText: Clara had taken to keeping herbs and bees behind her house. I visited one July afternoon without needing a bottle, an instrument, or a favor. She asked my opinion of a sickly plant. I pronounced on its leaves, twice and incorrectly, until she lifted a paving stone and showed me how the roots had been crowded. We moved the stone, drank warm tea, and watched bees make an industry of the thyme. I spoke of the lives I had brought forth. The plant recovered. On my next visit I brought a drawing of its roots, and she used the reverse of the paper to write a shopping list.

access.title: The Price of Coal
access.firstPersonText: At the university, coal had entered the cellar by an arrangement as natural and inexplicable as Providence. At the tower it came wet, late, and at a price which might have warmed us by outrage alone. I economized on heat until the King lost appetite and the Queen grew languid. Clara found a box of my cigars and laid it beside the fuel bill. She was offensively silent. I disposed of the cigars and bought coal. The creatures revived, though I shall not pretend that one evening establishes a complete theory of temperature. I recorded the readings beside the expense and put the empty cigar box away. For a week afterward I found myself seeking it at the usual hour. Habit is a petty tyrant, with none of the grandeur of an emperor.

access.title: The Coal Woman's Measure
access.firstPersonText: Rosa Brandl arrived with coal in a cart that shed black water over my threshold. I asked her to place three baskets beneath the east stairs and she declined until she had inspected the floor. It was rotten, she said, and she would not have the collapse of an aristocratic ruin attributed to her horse. I informed her that the place possessed no aristocracy except the intellectual kind. She placed the coal in the kitchen instead, where its dust settled upon my clean papers. Her measure was tin, deeply dented, and indisputably honest. I paid more than I had intended, then watched her carry the final basket without the assistance I had neglected to offer. For three winters afterward she knew my fuel expenditure more accurately than any surviving colleague knew my work. She never called me Professor. Curiously, I did not correct her.

access.title: The Coat on the Nail
access.firstPersonText: My professorial coat hung from a nail in the tower's stairwell because the damp made a wardrobe an architectural joke. I had worn it during the hearing and would not relinquish it merely because the university had reclaimed its keys. Clara found the lining spotted with mildew. She said she would have it dried and patched; I said the coat was perfectly serviceable. Lenz pointed out that the shoulders had begun to smell like a neglected cellar. I gave it over with a ceremony of offended dignity. Clara returned it three days later, the cuffs repaired with thread slightly darker than the original. I had worn it during the hearing and would not relinquish it merely because the university had reclaimed its keys. Clara found the lining spotted with mildew. She said she would have it dried and patched; I said the coat was perfectly serviceable. Lenz pointed out that the shoulders had begun to smell like a neglected cellar. I gave it over with a ceremony of offended dignity. Clara returned it three days later, the cuffs repaired with thread slightly darker than the original. At a time when every other article seemed to have changed its address or its owner, I found the coat in the same place each morning. I called this discipline. Clara called it a curious attachment to a poor nail. Neither description accounts for the fact that I put it on before answering official letters.

access.title: The Price of Coal
access.firstPersonText: At the university, coal had entered the cellar by an arrangement as natural and inexplicable as Providence. At the tower it came wet, late, and at a price which might have warmed us by outrage alone. I economized on heat until the King lost appetite and the Queen grew languid. Clara found a box of my cigars and laid it beside the fuel bill. She was offensively silent. I disposed of the cigars and bought coal. The creatures revived, though I shall not pretend that one evening establishes a complete theory of temperature. I recorded the readings beside the expense and put the empty cigar box away. For a week afterward I found myself seeking it at the usual hour. Habit is a petty tyrant, with none of the grandeur of an emperor.

access.title: The Coal Woman's Measure
access.firstPersonText: Rosa Brandl arrived with coal in a cart that shed black water over my threshold. I asked her to place three baskets beneath the east stairs and she declined until she had inspected the floor. It was rotten, she said, and she would not have the collapse of an aristocratic ruin attributed to her horse. I informed her that the place possessed no aristocracy except the intellectual kind. She placed the coal in the kitchen instead, where its dust settled upon my clean papers. Her measure was tin, deeply dented, and indisputably honest. I paid more than I had intended, then watched her carry the final basket without the assistance I had neglected to offer. For three winters afterward she knew my fuel expenditure more accurately than any surviving colleague knew my work. She never called me Professor. Curiously, I did not correct her.
